articleOptions.headline: Birch Aquarium Makes History with First-Ever Red Octopus Settlement
articleOptions.subHeadline: La Jolla's renowned aquarium achieves breakthrough in cephalopod care
articleOptions.content: La Jolla's Birch Aquarium has reached a historic milestone that has marine scientists buzzing worldwide. The team successfully settled more than 15 red octopuses, marking the first time this species has been hatched, raised, and settled in aquarium care. The achievement represents a major breakthrough in understanding one of the most mysterious phases of cephalopod life. The journey began last summer when Senior Aquarist Maddy Tracewell discovered a female red octopus guarding thousands of eggs behind the scenes. By October, those eggs hatched into thousands of tiny paralarvae, some no bigger than a grain of rice. When they first hatched, they looked like tiny aliens. Now they finally look like a real octopus, and I am so excited and amazed, Tracewell said. For months, the team worked tirelessly to replicate the pelagic ocean environment these creatures needed to survive. Octopus settlement remains one of the least understood phases in a cephalopod's life. Scientists have rarely observed the transition from free-swimming planktonic stage to the benthic settled lifestyle on the seafloor. During settlement, the octopus's arms develop fully, and the creature learns to use them for hunting and movement. This breakthrough at Birch Aquarium offers researchers a rare, detailed glimpse into these early life stages. Because no one had successfully settled this species before, Tracewell collaborated with marine researchers worldwide, including Dan Shigeki in Japan. With approximately 15 octopuses now settled at Birch, researchers are documenting everything they have learned. For locals, this achievement puts Birch Aquarium at Scripps Institution of Oceanography on the global map for marine research innovation, right in our own backyard.
